text: This is the southern Amazon region of South America, mapped from satellite data.
The coloured areas are places where tree cover that existed in the year two thousand was lost between two thousand and one and two thousand and twenty-four.
Yellow is early.
Red is recent.
Each pixel covers about thirty metres of ground.
Today we will use maps like this one to ask a simple question.
How much forest is being lost, and how do we know?
Forests cover four point one four billion hectares.
About one third of the land on Earth.
At least one point one eight billion hectares of that is classified as primary forest.
These figures come from the Food and Agriculture Organization's Global Forest Resources Assessment, published in October two thousand and twenty-five.
It covers two hundred and thirty-six countries and areas.
Mapping forests from space is not new.
NASA's first Landsat satellite launched on the twenty-third of July, nineteen seventy-two.
Since then, Landsat satellites have continuously acquired images of the Earth's land surface.
Today Europe's Sentinel-2 satellites add images at ten-metre resolution, revisiting the same ground about every five days.
A map is only as good as its definition.
In the global forest change dataset from the University of Maryland, tree cover means vegetation taller than five metres.
Loss means a stand-replacement disturbance, a change from forest to non-forest.
That definition matters.
It counts what satellites can see, which is not always the same as what a country calls deforestation.
There is no single number for deforestation, because there is no single question.
The FAO assessment is compiled with national correspondents from one hundred and ninety-seven countries and areas.
Global Forest Watch measures tree cover loss from satellites, and that includes loss from fire.
And Brazil's space agency, INPE, runs a programme called PRODES that measures deforestation in the Brazilian Legal Amazon only.
Those numbers should never be placed on one axis as if they measured the same thing.
In this film, each one will be labelled with its source.
Here is the good news, and it is real.
According to the FAO, deforestation slowed to ten point nine million hectares per year between two thousand fifteen and twenty twenty-five.
In the nineteen nineties it was seventeen point six.
Net forest loss fell from ten point seven million hectares per year in the nineteen nineties to four point one two million in twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-five.
But ten point nine million hectares a year is still a very large number.
The trend is falling.
The loss has not stopped.
Now the camera moves closer.
The dashed line is the Legal Amazon, the area INPE monitors.
Inside and outside it, the colours show the year of loss.
Every shade on this map was recorded in a dataset that anyone can download.
INPE publishes the same kind of detail for the Brazilian Legal Amazon.
Its yearly deforestation layer contains more than eight hundred thousand individual polygons, each with a date and an area.
For the year from August two thousand twenty-three to July two thousand twenty-four, INPE estimated six thousand two hundred and eighty-eight square kilometres of deforestation.
For the following year, the first estimate was five thousand seven hundred and ninety-six square kilometres.
After the data were consolidated in March two thousand twenty-six, the figure became five thousand seven hundred and thirty-one.
Notice that detail.
Even official numbers are revised, and a careful presentation says which version it is using.
Satellites also show that the story is not only about clearing.
Global Forest Watch reported that in two thousand twenty-four, the world lost six point seven million hectares of tropical primary forest, nearly twice as much as in two thousand twenty-three.
For the first time on record, fires, not agriculture, were the leading cause, at nearly fifty percent.
Brazil accounted for forty-two percent of that loss, and fires caused sixty-six percent of Brazil's.
In two thousand twenty-five, tropical primary forest loss fell by thirty-six percent, to four point three million hectares.
That is still forty-six percent higher than a decade earlier.
Across all kinds of tree cover, not only primary forest, the world lost about thirty million hectares in two thousand twenty-four, five percent more than the year before.
In two thousand twenty-five, global tree cover loss declined by fourteen percent, to twenty-five point five million hectares.
Fires were responsible for forty-two percent of it.
That is an area larger than the United Kingdom.
What do these maps tell us?
That forest loss can be measured, mapped, and published openly.
They also tell us the target is not met.
Global Forest Watch reports that deforestation in two thousand twenty-five was seventy percent higher than the level needed to halt and reverse forest loss by two thousand thirty.
A map cannot protect a forest.
But it can show us, pixel by pixel, whether we are keeping our promises.
Every number in this film comes from a public source, listed on screen.
The sources are the FAO, Global Forest Watch and the University of Maryland, INPE, NASA and the U S Geological Survey, and the European Space Agency.
Thank you.
